findings.title: Findings converge on project-phase state persisted in the result cache (D14 pending claims, D11 project entries)
findings.why_it_matters: Four findings from both critics land on one mechanism: the per-file result cache taking on project-phase data. That means D14's pending pragma claims (with owner spans) and D11's project-rule entries. Each finding attacks it from a different side:
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate project-phase state in the result cache before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions: does the project phase need to persist anything per file, given D3 hands it every loaded buffer? What does the read-once invariant actually guarantee (one disk read, or one parse)? What would D11 still buy once D14's coupling is settled? Is losing per-file pragma parsing on cache hits a real cost when HSL104 is opt-in?

findings.title: Findings converge on D16 finding identity
findings.why_it_matters: Three findings, from both critics, are about what D16's identity identifies and when it gets designed:
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate D16 finding identity before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions: does an identity name an occurrence or a cluster? Does #52 compare sets or multisets? What stays stable when a cluster gains a copy or a copy's span changes? Does this milestone's issue 6 need identity at all, or only #52's issue 7? How does the group id relate to identity once those are answered?

findings.title: D14 persists pending pragma claims in the cache, but the project phase already holds every file's bytes
findings.why_it_matters: D14-A is the ledger's most complex mechanism: rated "Highest" engine complexity and "hard" to reverse, it turns pragma claims into cacheable data. It exists to avoid re-parsing pragmas in the project phase, and it rejected B on "Read-once: Broken". But read-once is a disk-read invariant. The code reads and decodes every file before the cache lookup, and tokenizing and parsing are lazy. D3 already hands the project phase every file's loaded bytes. So re-deriving claims for the files that need them is a re-parse from memory, not a re-read. B's other weakness (pragmas in clean files go unreported) disappears if the project phase byte-greps every loaded buffer for project-rule ids instead of looking only at files with candidates.
findings.recommended: A: Replace D14-A's cached pending claims with project-phase derivation from the loaded buffers. Select files that have project-rule candidates or whose bytes contain a project-rule id, build their analysis layer from memory, and run the existing claim matching.

findings.title: Project-candidate ownership changes today's matching rule, and the cache-hit path lacks the data to keep it
findings.why_it_matters: Today a pragma claims a candidate when `candidate.owner == owner`, where the owner is the innermost statement enclosing the line. D15 says a duplicate occurrence matches "when its start line falls inside the owner statement, the same rule as Python". That is containment, not equality, so it isn't the same rule. Under containment, a trailing `ignore HSL104` on a `def` or `class` line (whose owner is the whole statement) hides every duplicate that starts anywhere in the body. That breaks D13's deciding factor: "a suppression only ever hides what it sits on". Keeping today's equality semantics needs, at project phase, each candidate's innermost statement at its start line. On a per-file cache hit the file was never parsed, so D14-A as written would need either a re-parse or a statement-span index in the cache entry. Neither is in D14's "entries grow by the pending claims". The `NO_OWNER` gap window in `_owns` has no stated project-rule analogue either.
findings.recommended: A: Match a project candidate by innermost-statement equality at its start line, the same `candidate_for_line` path file rules use, and correct D15's "falls inside" wording.

findings.title: Cluster-fragment identity can't tell a new 4th copy from an existing cluster, and drifts when membership changes
findings.why_it_matters: D16 keys the duplicate rule on a hash of the cluster's fragment, and D12 emits one finding per occurrence, so every occurrence in a cluster shares one identity. #52 reports head findings "whose identity is absent from the base tree". With 3 copies at base and 4 at head, the identity is the same, so the new copy passes. That is #52's flaw 1 in a new form, yet D16's table claims to fix it. The opposite also happens. The fragment comes from grouping overlapping jscpd pairs, so a new copy whose match is longer or shorter changes the grouped span and the hash, and then every existing occurrence reads as new.
findings.recommended: A: Key each occurrence on its own whitespace-normalized text, and have #52 compare occurrence counts per identity (multiset).

findings.title: "Unused suppression" is inferred from absent candidates; the finalizer isn't told when project output is incomplete
findings.why_it_matters: `apply_suppressions` reports an unused suppression only when `not claim.candidates and candidates_complete`. The flag exists because an empty candidate list is only evidence when the list is complete. D14 moves the "unused" verdict for project rules to a finalizer after the project phase, but says nothing about what the finalizer is told about completeness. In several cases absence isn't evidence: jscpd fails or times out, project candidates exceed the budget, or D10's explicit-path runs. The output could then carry a wall of false "unused suppression for HSL104" diagnostics alongside the operational error the Posture requires.
findings.recommended: A: The project phase returns an explicit completeness flag per project rule (mirroring `candidates_complete`). The finalizer issues "unused" verdicts only for complete rules, and on project-phase failure the output carries the operational error with no project-rule unused diagnostics.
findings.chosen: A: The project phase returns an explicit completeness flag per project rule (mirroring `candidates_complete`). The finalizer issues "unused" verdicts only for complete rules, and on project-phase failure the output carries the operational error with no project-rule unused diagnostics.
findings.choice_reason: Asked how peers handle it before choosing.

findings.title: "Does rule R apply to file F" now comes from three partial notions
findings.why_it_matters: Today "applies to this file" means one thing: the per-file `enabled_rules` after per-file-ignores, used by the cache key, detector selection, and the disabled-rule HSL900 diagnostic. The ledger adds two more notions without reconciling them:
findings.recommended: A: Define one `applies(rule, file)` from global selection, per-file-ignores, and file language. Discovery, detector dispatch, cache keys, project-file-set construction, and HSL900 all call it. A per-file-ignored file is removed from that project rule's input.
findings.chosen: A: Define one `applies(rule, file)` from global selection, per-file-ignores, and file language. Discovery, detector dispatch, cache keys, project-file-set construction, and HSL900 all call it. A per-file-ignored file is removed from that project rule's input.

findings.title: TypeScript statement ownership has no grammar contract or parse-error policy
findings.why_it_matters: D15-B promises TypeScript pragmas with "statement ownership", but tree-sitter has no "statement" abstraction. Much of what jscpd flags in TypeScript isn't a statement: class members, object-literal methods, JSX elements, decorators, `export` wrappers. `tree-sitter-typescript` also ships two grammars (`typescript` and `tsx`) that parse differently. Tree-sitter is error-tolerant, so a file with a syntax error, or with syntax newer than the grammar, yields a tree with `ERROR` nodes rather than a load error. Python files take the `SourceFile.error` path today, and the ledger gives TypeScript no equivalent. Combined with Finding 4's containment wording, a member-level pragma that resolves to the enclosing class would suppress everything inside it.
findings.recommended: B: Define the same owner table, but on `ERROR` nodes disable pragmas for that file with one HSL900 diagnostic and keep its duplicate findings.
findings.choice_reason: Asked whether another parser exists; none is maintained on PyPI besides tree-sitter, so kept B and required a maintained grammar package.

findings.title: Cache hash inputs are hard-coded per rule; D5 removes the options tuple without saying how a rule contributes to the hash
findings.why_it_matters: `hash_effective_config` takes `hsl101`, `hsl102`, and `hsl103` as named parameters. It has a rule-specific special case (the filename is folded in only when an HSL101 family scopes to filenames) and a parser input (`python_version`). D5 replaces the options tuple with rule-declared types, but neither D5 nor Breakdown issue 3 says how a declared rule contributes its options, or any extra input like the filename, to the per-file config hash. Issue 3 will hit this immediately.
findings.chosen: Add to Breakdown item 3: "Each rule declares its contribution to the per-file config hash: its options, plus any extra input such as HSL101's filename when a family scopes to filenames. `hash_effective_config` is assembled from the registry rather than from one parameter per rule."

findings.title: D12's group id duplicates D16's identity for the duplicate rule
findings.why_it_matters: D12-B adds a `related` list and a shared group id, plus a `schema_version` bump. D16-A adds an identity to every finding, and for the duplicate rule that identity hashes the cluster's fragment, so all occurrences share it. As written, the group id is a second name for identity on this rule, and two overlapping fields invite a "which do I key on" question from the first JSON consumer. The redundancy only holds while identity stays cluster-level: if Finding 5 or Finding 11 changes identity, the group id stops being redundant.
findings.recommended: C: Keep D12-B as ratified until Finding 2/5/11 settles what identity names.

findings.title: D16 designs identity from one rule, ahead of its only consumer, and leaves the field's status unstated
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger defines the identity field and the duplicate rule's key in issue 6, and defers every other rule's key to #52 (issue 7, the same milestone). The abstraction (rule id plus rule-supplied key) is designed from one data point. A key shape that suits a content-hash cluster may not suit path-plus-symbol findings, and D16 itself notes other rules key differently. D16 also doesn't say whether the field is required or optional in issue 6. A required field with no key for seven rules forces placeholders, while an optional one means #52 retrofits the schema.
findings.recommended: A: Move the identity field and the duplicate rule's key from issue 6 to issue 7 (#52), designed together with the other rules' keys.

findings.title: D5's declared-options migration is the least load-bearing part of issue 3
findings.why_it_matters: D5-B is justified mostly by #53 adding a fifth and sixth options member, and #53 is out of this milestone. The friction it removes is real: three cast adapters, a hash function with a parameter per rule, and a config branch per rule. But it migrates three working rules and the config parser inside an issue that also adds the second rule kind and the project phase.

findings.title: Parse-derived claims are cached, but parser package versions aren't in the cache key
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: solo maintainer with pinned versions; the failure is rare but silent. D14-A stores parse-derived TypeScript pragma claims in the per-file cache entry, keyed on content and config. `code_identity()` covers only house-lint's own sources, so upgrading `tree-sitter` or `tree-sitter-typescript` (core dependencies under D20) can change statement boundaries without changing the key. Stale claims are then replayed for unchanged files. Python already folds `python_version` into the config hash for exactly this reason.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: after a TypeScript parser upgrade, cached pragma claims can be stale until the cache is cleared.

findings.title: D11 caches project-rule results, which helps only runs on an unchanged tree
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a solo maintainer running jscpd (3-4s on hassette) from pre-push. D11's own table says hook runs "always miss", and the motivating use is a hook. The only beneficiary is consecutive `check` runs on an untouched tree. It adds an entry type and a set-keyed hash over every file in scope, and any bug in that key (for example a path set that misses part of D10's full scope) becomes a stale-result bug. D11's own Pick-B clause ties it to D14's complexity.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: D11's project cache helps only repeated runs on an unchanged tree, and hook runs always miss.

findings.title: D20 puts tree-sitter in the core install, partly on an overstated error-path cost
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a solo maintainer. Install size matters little here, which is why this is not higher. D20-A's main reason is future per-file TypeScript rules, and the only named example (hassette #1911) closed as a draft. The table's "Missing-parser error path to build: Yes" for B overstates the cost. TypeScript enters a scan only when HSL104 is enabled (D6), and HSL104 already fails loudly when its extra is missing (D8), so checking the parser is one more line in the same preflight. B's real cost is the no-lazy-imports rule: an optional parser would have to be imported conditionally. D20's recommendation mentions module-level imports, but the table doesn't use that as the reason against B. Every Python-only run pays tree-sitter's import cost and carries two native wheels.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: every install carries the parser wheels and every run pays its import cost.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: every install carries the parser wheels and every run pays its import cost.

findings.title: Line coordinates between house-lint and jscpd are agreed only by assumption
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: unusual line endings or non-ASCII source; unverified against jscpd, which I did not run. House-lint's line model decodes with universal newlines and splits on `\n` only, and suppression matching (D13, D15) uses the occurrence's start line. jscpd reports line and column from its own tokenizer over the real file (D9-C). Any disagreement (bare `\r`, form feed, BOM, tab or multibyte columns) shifts the start line, and the pragma match misses. The miss is loud rather than silent: the finding still shows, plus an "unused suppression" diagnostic.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: on files with bare `\r`, form feeds, or a BOM, a jscpd start line can disagree with house-lint's and a pragma can miss.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: on files with bare `\r`, form feeds, or a BOM, a jscpd start line can disagree with house-lint's and a pragma can miss.
